## Story

> Friday night at Vossberg & Daughters, auctioneers since 1896. At 06:00 the printer starts on the catalogue for Saturday's sale of vintage watches, and eight lots still have no estimate.
>
> Konrad Albers, who priced every watch in this house for 31 years, retired last month, and his pricing spreadsheet died with his laptop. What the house still has: the records of 1,200 watches sold in the last four years, his notes on the walls, and a rumour that one of those sales was a forgery.
>
> Teach a model what a watch is worth. This room loads Python with pandas and scikit-learn, so the first puzzle you open takes a little while.

## Stations

### 1. The rule of thumb

**Practises:** Simple linear regression: X as a table with one column, fit, coef_ and intercept_  
**Needs:** 🔎 Albers's graph paper  
**Data:** [sales.py](../../content/rooms/ml-auction/data/sales.py)

**Task:**

> Konrad Albers priced watches for Vossberg & Daughters for 31 years. His spreadsheet died with his laptop, but his first rule of thumb is still pinned above his desk: a straight line on graph paper, the hammer price against the condition grade. The number beside it is smudged.
>
> The last four years of sales are loaded as `sales`, one row per watch sold, indexed by lot number: its age in years, the maker's tier (1 = no-name, 5 = the great houses), the case diameter in mm, the condition grade (1 = worn, 5 = as new), whether box and papers came with it (`box_papers`), the movement and the hammer price in euros (`price`).
>
> 1. Fit a straight line through all sales: `price` against `condition`.
> 2. Enter how many euros one condition grade adds, rounded to whole euros.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

# sales is loaded: 1,200 watches sold in the last four years, indexed by lot number.
print(sales.head())

model = LinearRegression().fit(sales["condition"], sales["price"])
print(model.coef_, model.intercept_)
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

model = LinearRegression().fit(sales[["condition"]], sales["price"])
print(model.coef_[0], model.intercept_)
print(round(model.coef_[0]))
```

**Answer:** `274`

**Reveals when solved:**

> **274 € per grade.** Albers's line starts at 800 € (at a grade 0 that no watch has) and climbs 274 € with every grade.
>
> scikit-learn always wants a table of features, even with only one column: `sales[["condition"]]` (a DataFrame) instead of `sales["condition"]` (a Series). The fitted line is then `intercept_ + coef_ × grade`.
>
> One line for every watch, though: 274 € is a fortune for a 300 € quartz watch and nothing for a 20,000 € antique.

**Hints:**

1. Run the starter and read the error: scikit-learn expected a 2D array. What shape is `sales["condition"]`?
2. Double brackets select a DataFrame with one column: `sales[["condition"]]`. The target stays a Series.
3. `model = LinearRegression().fit(sales[["condition"]], sales["price"])`; `model.coef_[0]` is the euros per grade.

### 2. Last year's estimates

**Practises:** Regression metrics: MAE, RMSE and R² with sklearn.metrics, why errors must not cancel, a mean baseline  
**Needs:** 🔎 Ilse Vossberg's memo  
**Data:** [sales.py](../../content/rooms/ml-auction/data/sales.py)

**Task:**

> Before the house copies Albers's methods, Ilse Vossberg wants to know whether they were any good. On the ledger table lies last autumn's sale sheet: for each of its 120 lots, Albers's printed estimate and the hammer price, loaded as `last_sale`.
>
> 1. Measure how far his estimates were from the hammer prices: store `mae`, `rmse` and `r2`.
> 2. Store as `baseline_mae` how far off the cheapest appraiser in town would have been, the one in Ilse's memo.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score

print(last_sale.head())   # last autumn's 120 lots
hammer = last_sale["hammer"]       # what the watch sold for
estimate = last_sale["estimate"]   # what Albers printed in the catalogue

mae = (hammer - estimate).mean()
print(f"Albers was off by {mae:.0f} € per lot on average")

rmse = None
r2 = None
baseline_mae = None   # the cheapest appraiser in town
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score

hammer = last_sale["hammer"]
estimate = last_sale["estimate"]

mae = mean_absolute_error(hammer, estimate)
rmse = mean_squared_error(hammer, estimate) ** 0.5
r2 = r2_score(hammer, estimate)
baseline_mae = mean_absolute_error(hammer, [hammer.mean()] * len(hammer))
print(round(mae, 1), round(rmse, 1), round(r2, 3), round(baseline_mae, 1))
```

**Checked result** (`_estimates_check(mae, rmse, r2, baseline_mae)`):

```json
"appraised"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> Albers missed by **256 €** per lot on average (MAE), not by 34 €: the starter let misses up and down cancel out. His RMSE is 436 €: squaring first makes a few big misses weigh more, so RMSE is never below MAE. His R² is 0.90.
>
> Guessing last autumn's mean hammer price (1,459 €) for every lot misses by 952 €. That guess is the baseline every model has to beat, and its R² is 0 by definition: R² says what share of the baseline's squared misses a model gets rid of. Albers earned his fee.

**Hints:**

1. Positive and negative misses cancel in `(hammer - estimate).mean()`. MAE averages their sizes: `mean_absolute_error(hammer, estimate)`.
2. RMSE is the square root of `mean_squared_error(hammer, estimate)`. `r2_score` takes the truth first: `r2_score(hammer, estimate)`.
3. The cheapest appraiser guesses `hammer.mean()` for every lot: `baseline_mae = mean_absolute_error(hammer, [hammer.mean()] * len(hammer))`.

### 3. The long tail

**Practises:** A right-skewed target: fitting on np.log, back-transforming with np.exp, MAE on a test split, reading log coefficients as percentages  
**Needs:** 🔎 The histogram on the wall, 🔎 The house rule for valuations  
**Data:** [sales.py](../../content/rooms/ml-auction/data/sales.py)

**Task:**

> A bar chart of every hammer price hangs on the saleroom wall: a tall hump of cheap watches and a thin tail of dear ones. Albers's assistant drew it, and wrote a note under it.
>
> 1. Split the sales as the house rule says.
> 2. Fit `LinearRegression` on the numeric columns twice: once on the price, once on the log of the price. Score both on the test part, in euros, as `mae_linear` and `mae_log`.
> 3. In the log model, how much does one condition grade add to the price? Store it in percent as `percent`.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from helpers import show_hist

show_hist(sales["price"], bins=40, title="Hammer prices")

X = sales[["age", "maker_tier", "case_mm", "condition", "box_papers"]]   # the numeric columns
y = sales["price"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y)   # see the house rule

linear = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
mae_linear = mean_absolute_error(y_test, linear.predict(X_test))
print("linear:", round(mae_linear), "€")

mae_log = None   # the same model fitted on np.log(y_train), scored in euros
percent = None   # what one condition grade adds in the log model, in percent
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from helpers import show_hist

show_hist(sales["price"], bins=40, title="Hammer prices")
X = sales[["age", "maker_tier", "case_mm", "condition", "box_papers"]]
y = sales["price"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=6)

linear = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
mae_linear = mean_absolute_error(y_test, linear.predict(X_test))

log_model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, np.log(y_train))
mae_log = mean_absolute_error(y_test, np.exp(log_model.predict(X_test)))
percent = (np.exp(log_model.coef_[3]) - 1) * 100
print(round(mae_linear), round(mae_log), round(percent, 1))
```

**Checked result** (`_tail_check(mae_linear, mae_log, percent)`):

```json
"tamed"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> On the log of the price the model misses test lots by **717 €** instead of 971 €. In euros, the few dear watches pull every coefficient towards them, and the line even predicts negative prices for 23 cheap test lots.
>
> On the log scale every feature multiplies the price instead of adding euros: **one condition grade adds 16 %**, to a 300 € quartz watch and to a 20,000 € antique alike. A log coefficient `b` reads as `np.exp(b) - 1`; for small `b` that is close to `b` itself. Predictions come back to euros with `np.exp`.

**Hints:**

1. The house rule gives the split: `train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=6)`. Then `log_model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, np.log(y_train))`.
2. The log model predicts log euros. `np.exp(log_model.predict(X_test))` turns them back into euros; compare those with `y_test`.
3. `condition` is the fourth column, so its coefficient is `log_model.coef_[3]`; `percent = (np.exp(log_model.coef_[3]) - 1) * 100`.

### 4. The movement

**Practises:** Multiple regression: one-hot encoding with pd.get_dummies, reading coefficients all else equal, omitted-variable bias  
**Needs:** 3. The long tail (its result), 🔒 1. The rule of thumb, 🔎 The card in the display case  
**Data:** [sales.py](../../content/rooms/ml-auction/data/sales.py)

**Code lock** (opens with `274`):

> The display case has a three-digit combination lock. A brass tag hangs from it: "Combination = Albers's rule of thumb, in euros per condition grade."

**Task:**

> The display case by the window holds the house's teaching collection: one automatic, one hand-wound and one quartz watch, each with its box and papers, and a card about the three kinds of movement. Albers always told consignors that box and papers add a third to the price. Ilse doubts it.
>
> 1. Fit the log model on all sales with every column, the movement included. `LinearRegression` can't read words: encode the movement.
> 2. Store what box and papers add to the price, in percent, as `box_percent`. Compare it with a model that leaves the movement out.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X = sales.drop(columns="price")   # every column, the movement included
y = sales["price"]                # the target: see the long tail

model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
print(pd.Series(model.coef_, index=X.columns).round(3))

box_percent = None   # what box and papers add to the price, in percent
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X = pd.get_dummies(sales.drop(columns="price"), dtype=int)
y = np.log(sales["price"])
model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
coefs = pd.Series(model.coef_, index=X.columns)
print(((np.exp(coefs) - 1) * 100).round(1))
box_percent = (np.exp(coefs["box_papers"]) - 1) * 100

numeric = X.drop(columns=["movement_automatic", "movement_manual", "movement_quartz"])
without = LinearRegression().fit(numeric, y)
print("without the movement:", round((np.exp(without.coef_[4]) - 1) * 100, 1))
```

**Checked result** (`_movement_check(box_percent)`):

```json
"wound"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> With the movement in the model, box and papers add **14 %**, not the 37 % a model without the movement claims, and not Albers's third. Papers survive more often with automatics, and automatics fetch far more than quartz watches: left out of the model, the movement's effect was credited to the papers. That is omitted-variable bias.
>
> `pd.get_dummies` turns the word column into one 0/1 column per word. With an intercept one of them is redundant, and `drop_first=True` drops it; the other coefficients stay the same either way. Quartz costs 45 % less than an automatic, all else equal.

**Hints:**

1. The error says it can't convert `'automatic'` to a number. `pd.get_dummies(X, dtype=int)` replaces the movement column with one 0/1 column per kind. And the target should be `np.log(y)`, as at the long tail.
2. `coefs = pd.Series(model.coef_, index=X.columns)` names the coefficients. A log coefficient `b` adds `(np.exp(b) - 1) * 100` percent.
3. `X = pd.get_dummies(sales.drop(columns="price"), dtype=int)`, `model = LinearRegression().fit(X, np.log(y))`, then `box_percent = (np.exp(coefs["box_papers"]) - 1) * 100`. For the comparison, fit again without the movement columns.

### 5. The suspicious lot

**Practises:** Residuals: finding the case a model explains worst, why residuals in euros favour expensive items and log residuals don't  
**Needs:** 3. The long tail (its result), 🔒 2. Last year's estimates, 🔎 The evening paper  
**Data:** [sales.py](../../content/rooms/ml-auction/data/sales.py)

**Code lock** (opens with `256`):

> The drawer of the watchmaker's bench, where the re-examination files are kept, has a three-digit lock. A note in the workshop's pencil: "Code = how many euros Albers missed per lot last autumn, on average (MAE), in whole euros."

**Task:**

> The newspaper on the coffee table carries the story: a forged watch went through Vossberg's spring sale. Since then the workshop has re-examined every watch the house sold, so `sales` records what each watch really is, not what the bidders believed. Somewhere in it is a sale that its features can't explain.
>
> 1. Fit a model of the price on the watches' features and compute each sale's residual.
> 2. Find the sale that lies furthest above what its features justify. Store its lot number as `lot`.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from helpers import show_scatter

X = sales[["age", "maker_tier", "case_mm", "condition", "box_papers"]]
y = sales["price"]
model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)

residuals = y - model.predict(X)   # how far each sale lies above its prediction
print(residuals.sort_values(ascending=False).head(3))
show_scatter(model.predict(X), residuals, xlabel="predicted", ylabel="residual", title="Residuals")

lot = None   # the lot number of the forgery
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from helpers import show_scatter

X = pd.get_dummies(sales.drop(columns="price"), dtype=int)
y = np.log(sales["price"])
model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)

residuals = y - model.predict(X)
print(residuals.sort_values(ascending=False).head(3).round(2))
show_scatter(model.predict(X), residuals, xlabel="predicted (log)", ylabel="residual (log)", title="Residuals")
lot = residuals.idxmax()
print(sales.loc[lot])
```

**Checked result** (`_forgery_check(lot)`):

```json
"forged"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> **Lot 1964**: a 14-year-old quartz watch by a no-name maker, grade 2, no papers. Its features say about 170 €; it hammered at 8,400 €, 50 times as much. In log terms its residual is 3.9; no other sale is off by more than 1.1, a factor of 3.
>
> In euros, the largest residuals were genuine watches: lots 1467, 2066 and 1913, antiques of the great houses, where a miss of 10 % is thousands of euros. On the log scale every residual is a ratio, so the cheap forgery stands out. The house will refund the buyer, and lot 1964 has no place in the model for the catalogue.

**Hints:**

1. The starter's top three are dear antiques by the great houses: in euros, a small share of a big price is a big residual. Which target did the long tail recommend?
2. Fit on `np.log(y)` and take `residuals = np.log(y) - model.predict(X)`. The movement helps too: `pd.get_dummies(sales.drop(columns="price"), dtype=int)`.
3. `lot = residuals.idxmax()` is the index label, the lot number, of the largest residual.

### 6. The catalogue (Final lock)

**Practises:** Putting it together: a log target, one-hot encoding, a squared feature with PolynomialFeatures found from residuals, the same columns for new data, predictions back in euros  
**Needs:** 5. The suspicious lot (its result), 4. The movement (its result), 3. The long tail (its result), 🔒 5. The suspicious lot, 🔎 The insurer's letter, 🔎 The watchmaker's note  
**Data:** [sales.py](../../content/rooms/ml-auction/data/sales.py)

**Code lock** (opens with `196414`):

> The press is locked with a six-digit PIN. Ilse's note on the cover: "PIN = the forged lot's number, then what box and papers really add, in whole percent."

**Task:**

> The proof of Saturday's catalogue lies on the press, with eight empty estimate fields. `catalogue` holds the eight lots, indexed by lot number, with the same columns as `sales`, in the printer's order. The press starts at 06:00.
>
> 1. Build the house's valuation model from everything you learned tonight. Before you trust it, plot its residuals against age: the watchmaker's note says why.
> 2. Store an estimate in euros for each lot as `estimates`: a list in the catalogue's order, or a Series indexed by lot number.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from helpers import show_scatter

print(catalogue)   # Saturday's eight lots, indexed by lot number

X = pd.get_dummies(sales.drop(columns="price"), dtype=int)
y = np.log(sales["price"])
model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)

# show_scatter(sales["age"], y - model.predict(X), xlabel="age", ylabel="residual (log)", title="Residuals by age")

estimates = None   # one estimate in euros per catalogue lot
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from helpers import show_scatter


def features(df):
    X = pd.get_dummies(df, dtype=int)
    X["age2"] = X["age"] ** 2
    return X


genuine = sales.drop(1964)
X = features(genuine.drop(columns="price"))
y = np.log(genuine["price"])
model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
show_scatter(genuine["age"], y - model.predict(X), xlabel="age", ylabel="residual (log)", title="Residuals by age")

C = features(catalogue)[X.columns]
estimates = pd.Series(np.exp(model.predict(C)), index=catalogue.index).round(-1)
print(estimates)
```

**Checked result** (`_catalogue_check(estimates)`):

```json
"printed"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> The insurer's fax comes back at 05:41: all eight estimates accepted. The nearly new lot 2201 is printed at about 4,600 €, the 88-year-old lot 2202 at about 4,000 €, and the quartz lot 2203 at about 400 €.
>
> The residuals told you what the straight line in age missed: young watches and antiques both fetch more than the 30-to-40-year-olds in between. A squared age lets a linear model bend, and it is still linear regression, linear in its coefficients. The press starts at six. Albers's graph paper goes into a frame beside the case clock: one line for every watch, 31 years long.

**Hints:**

1. Uncomment the plot: the residuals form a U over age, too low for young and old watches. Add the age squared as a column: `X["age2"] = X["age"] ** 2`, or `PolynomialFeatures(2)` on `X[["age"]]`. Leave out the forged lot: `sales.drop(1964)`.
2. The catalogue needs the same columns in the same order: `C = pd.get_dummies(catalogue, dtype=int)`, add `age2` the same way, then `C = C[X.columns]`.
3. The model predicts log euros: `estimates = pd.Series(np.exp(model.predict(C)), index=catalogue.index)`.

## Clues in the room

### 🔎 Albers's graph paper

*Used by: 1. The rule of thumb*

> A yellowed sheet of graph paper in a clip frame. Across the bottom: **condition grade 1 2 3 4 5**. Up the side: **hammer price, €**. A dozen pencil crosses and one straight line drawn through them with a ruler.
>
> Beside the line: "+ ▒▒▒ € per grade". The number is smudged by a thumb.
>
> At the bottom, in ink: "One line for every watch. — K. A., 1995"

### 🔎 Ilse Vossberg's memo

*Used by: 2. Last year's estimates*

> On the house's letterhead, in green ink:
>
> "An appraiser earns his fee only if he beats the cheapest appraiser in town: the one who writes **the sale's average hammer price** under every lot and goes home. Measure them both by how far they miss, in euros, and don't let a miss upwards cancel a miss downwards.
>
> And look at the big misses separately. One bad estimate costs us a consignor. — I. V."

### 🔎 The histogram on the wall

*Used by: 3. The long tail*

> A bar chart pinned to the wall: the hammer prices of four years. Three quarters of the watches sold below 2,000 €, in a tall hump of bars on the left. To the right a thin tail runs out past 25,000 €, a single bar here and there.
>
> Written underneath, in Albers's assistant's hand: "Nobody pays a fixed sum for a better grade. They pay **a share more**, on a cheap watch and on a dear one. — F."

### 🔎 The house rule for valuations

*Used by: 3. The long tail*

> VOSSBERG & DAUGHTERS · rule 4, valuations
>
> A valuation model is judged on lots it has not seen. Hold back a fifth of the sales as the test part (**test_size=0.2**), with **random_state=6**, the hour the printer starts, so that everyone gets the same split.
>
> Judge it in **euros**: that is what the bidders pay.

### 🔎 The card in the display case

*Used by: 4. The movement*

> THE HOUSE'S TEACHING COLLECTION · three movements
>
> **automatic**: wound by the swing of the wrist. Collectors' favourite.
> **manual**: wound by hand every morning. The oldest kind; a little dearer than an automatic, all else equal.
> **quartz**: a battery and a crystal, made since 1969. Accurate, cheap, and the least wanted at auction.
>
> Workshop note at the bottom: "Most automatics come to us with their box and papers. Most quartz watches come in a plastic bag."

### 🔎 The evening paper

*Used by: 5. The suspicious lot*

> KLEEBERGER ABENDBLATT
>
> **Forged watch sold at Vossberg's spring sale**
>
> A bidder paid thousands for a watch that turned out to be a cheap quartz movement in a fake case and dial. "It looked like nothing special on paper," a dealer said. "Its price was the only thing about it that made no sense." The auction house has had its workshop re-examine every watch it sold in the last four years and recorded what each one really is.

### 🔎 The insurer's letter

*Used by: 6. The catalogue*

> HALLBERG FINE ART INSURANCE
>
> Dear Ms Vossberg, as every season we will check the estimates in your catalogue against our own valuation model before the sale. We accept an estimate that lies **within 10 %** of our valuation. Estimates further off we cannot insure, and the lot will be withdrawn.
>
> Our model is built on the hammer prices of your past sales, as recorded by your workshop, **forgeries excluded**.

### 🔎 The watchmaker's note

*Used by: 6. The catalogue*

> Taped to the case clock, in the workshop's pencil:
>
> "Ilse, for the catalogue: don't price by age in a straight line. The **young** ones still sell on fashion, the **antiques** on rarity. Nobody wants the ones in between, the thirty- and forty-year-olds. — Tomasz"

## Handbook in the room: 📖 The house's valuation binder

**Fitting a line:** [`LinearRegression()`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression.html), [`model.fit(X, y)  model.predict(X)`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/getting_started.html#fitting-and-predicting-estimator-basics), [`pd.Series(model.coef_, index=X.columns)`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.html), [`train_test_split(X, y, test_size=, random_state=)`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.model_selection.train_test_split.html)
